Kurepa himself, and later Slavić, showed that this discrete sequence admits a natural analytic continuation to the whole complex plane (with the exception of the negative integers) via the integral representation

K(z) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-t}\,\frac{t^{z}-1}{t-1}\,dt ,

# Kurepa's Function and Petojević's Contributions to Its Study

Đuro Kurepa (1907–1993) was one of the most influential Serbian mathematicians of the twentieth century, whose work spanned set theory, topology, and number theory. Among his many contributions, one of the most enduring is what has come to be known as the **Kurepa function**, sometimes called the "left factorial," denoted !n. This function is defined as:

$$!n = 0! + 1! + 2! + \cdots + (n-1)!$$

Kurepa introduced this function in the 1970s and used it to formulate what is now known as **Kurepa's hypothesis** (or Kurepa's conjecture), which concerns the greatest common divisor of !n and n!. Specifically, the conjecture states that for every integer n ≥ 2, the greatest common divisor of !n and n! is equal to 2. This deceptively simple statement has proven remarkably difficult to prove or disprove, and it remains an open problem in number theory to this day, having been verified computationally for very large values of n without a general proof emerging.

Kurepa's broader mathematical legacy also includes significant work in set theory, where his name is attached to concepts such as **Kurepa trees**—structures of great importance in the study of infinite combinatorics and the foundations of set theory, particularly in relation to questions independent of the standard axioms (ZFC).

Building on Kurepa's foundational work, the mathematician **Aleksandar Petojević** has made substantial contributions to the further development and generalization of the Kurepa function. Petojević's research has focused on extending the left factorial function into more general mathematical frameworks, exploring its analytic properties, and investigating generalizations that connect it to other special functions in mathematics. His work includes studies on generalized factorial functions and their relationships to gamma functions, Bernoulli numbers, and other classical objects in analysis and number theory.

Petojević has published several papers examining variations of the Kurepa function, proposing new generalized forms (sometimes denoted with additional parameters) that preserve key properties of the original definition while extending its applicability to broader classes of problems. His work has helped keep Kurepa's ideas alive within the contemporary mathematical literature, ensuring that this area of research—rooted in Serbian mathematical tradition—continues to develop and attract interest from researchers working in combinatorics, number theory, and special functions.

Together, the work of Kurepa and the continuing research by Petojević illustrate how a single elegant mathematical idea can generate decades of inquiry, giving rise to open problems, generalizations, and a lasting legacy within a national mathematical school. The Kurepa function stands today as a modest yet compelling example of how simple definitions can lead to deep and still-unresolved mathematical questions.
